decision: compile every program at startup with compileAsync and hold frames until a fence passes
why: mantra 5 (when they're not looking): link programs while the worker grows the tree
result: rejected: SwiftShader has no KHR_parallel_shader_compile, the fence passes before ANGLE finishes linking, so the first draw waited on every program at once; compiling during generation also competes with the worker for the 4 CPU cores

decision: same, but query one program per task so each wait covers one link
why: split the link waits under 100 ms each
evidence: scratchpad/pr7/f2b/summary.json: longest 706 dotfiles, 872 linux; first query waits 690-790 ms
result: rejected: the command buffer is FIFO, so the first query waits for every compile queued before it, and single SwiftShader links still take 100-260 ms

decision: history core is sampled tree snapshots: ~50-80 commits found with /commits?until= (weekly 26 weeks, monthly to 2 years, yearly before, plus the root), each read with /git/trees/{tree}?recursive=1 and diffed by blob and tree sha
why: owner direction: one request per commit cannot scale (Linux has 1.3M commits); snapshots cost roughly the same for any repo and give last-changed, churn, born, gone and dead wood

decision: per-commit detail only for the newest 100 non-merge commits (DETAIL_COMMITS), giving exact recent dates, commit counts and author attribution
why: precise recent activity and owners without spending the hourly budget on old commits

decision: snapshots processed newest to oldest with a per-path accumulator [newest, oldest, version-oldest, churn, sha]
why: the head tree comes first, so the sample count and the head path set are known before any old tree is read, and contiguity needs no stored previous tree

decision: truncated recursive trees (over 100k entries or 7 MB) are re-read per top-level folder, reusing any top-level subtree whose sha matches the newer snapshot without a request; a split budget caps this and further truncated snapshots are skipped and marked partial
why: Linux's head tree is over 100k entries; reuse keeps the split cost to the folders that changed

decision: long jobs run as resumable steps: each request advances one bounded step (STEP_REQUESTS subrequests, STEP_ENTRIES tree entries), progress lives in KV, the reply is {status:pending, progress} until ready
why: a free Worker allows 50 subrequests and 10 ms CPU per request; steps are deterministic, so two polls racing on one step write the same state

decision: no lock on job state; KV last-write-wins and steps are idempotent, so a race only repeats work. Durable Objects would serialize it but tie the core to Cloudflare
why: keep the core host-agnostic and simple

decision: per-IP cap of 10 new (uncached) repos an hour in KV; cached repos unlimited; the [[ratelimits]] binding holds every IP to 60 requests a minute
why: owner direction: fairness and abuse guard; KV is eventually consistent so it is a guard, not an exact count
evidence: server/src/worker.ts takeQuota; test/worker.test.ts caps new repos

decision: a spent GitHub budget answers pending with retryAfter at the reset, not an error, and the job resumes from KV
why: owner direction: the client shows a calm growing state, and no work is lost
evidence: server/src/core/service.ts errorReply; test waits for the token budget

decision: cron prewarm: one job step for one PREWARM repo every ten minutes, round robin, using GITHUB_TOKEN only
why: owner direction: keep popular repos warm; one step per tick stays inside one invocation's subrequest limit

decision: superseded the single server token: visitors sign in with a GitHub OAuth App (no scopes); an uncached computation runs on the visitor's bearer token for that request only, never stored or logged; signed-out visitors get cached history or {status:needs-auth}
why: owner direction: one shared token does not scale; results come from public data so sharing them in KV is safe

decision: a GitHub 401 is an unauthorized reply with nothing written; /repos/{o}/{r} is now always read so private repos answer error private and nothing about them is stored; the negative cache for missing repos was dropped
why: a bad token must not poison the cache, and a 404 cached from one visitor could hide a repo from another
evidence: server/src/core/service.ts lookUp; tests refuses a token, never computes a private repo

decision: the token returns to the app by postMessage from a popup callback page addressed to the origin saved with the state, instead of a redirect back with the token in the URL
why: keeps the token out of every URL and history entry, and leaves the app's own hash link (repo and settings) untouched; state is single-use in KV for ten minutes
evidence: server/src/core/oauth.ts; test signs in through a popup

decision: the browser-run core with a pasted personal token (coordinator item 3) is not built

decision: the history Worker computes nothing: a signed-in visitor's browser runs the engine with their own token and uploads the gzipped History; the Worker checks and stores it, one KV write per accepted upload, no job state, no cron, no server token
why: the free plan allows 10 ms CPU, 50 subrequests and 1,000 KV writes a day shared with another project; the old step job wrote KV every step and Linux needed the paid plan
evidence: server/src/worker.ts; server/test/worker.test.ts (one write per upload, 7 GitHub requests per PUT)

decision: the Worker never opens an upload's body; it checks a manifest (head, every snapshot's sha, time and tree) against GitHub with the uploader's token: /user, /repos (public), the branch head, and /git/commits for the head plus 3 random snapshots
why: unpacking and parsing Linux's 0.86 MB gz / 8.15 MB JSON costs about 60 ms of CPU, six times the limit; the manifest checks cost 1.85 ms
evidence: node server/scripts/worker-cpu.mjs: PUT 1.85 ms Linux, 0.88 ms vite; GET 0.75 ms Linux

decision: the stored body is bound to its manifest by a SHA-256 digest of the snapshots' sha and time; readers drop a body whose repo, branch, head, count or digest disagree
why: the Worker cannot parse the body, so the reader enforces that it is the history the Worker checked

decision: per-path data (dates, churn, authors, CODEOWNERS teams, paths) in an upload is the uploader's word; unpicked snapshots and ancestry are unchecked; a fork-network commit can pass git/commits; the first upload for a head wins until the branch moves
why: the history is cosmetic data about a public repo, the tree itself comes from GitHub, and no token or private data is exposed; the uploader's login is kept in the metadata and the owner can delete the key
evidence: server/README.md What a forged upload can and cannot do

decision: OAuth state is an HMAC-signed (origin, 10-minute expiry, nonce) token instead of a KV record
why: sign-in costs no KV writes; GitHub's code is single use, so replaying a state within 10 minutes gains nothing
evidence: server/src/core/oauth.ts; server/test/worker.test.ts forged and expired state refused

decision: uploads are capped at 8 MiB, 2 a minute and 6 an hour per IP, and 300 a day in all; the hourly and daily counters live in the Cache API per data center
why: ten times Linux's body; keeps the account's shared 1,000 KV writes a day safe without spending writes on counting
evidence: server/wrangler.toml; server/test/worker.test.ts size cap and rate limits

decision: the sign-in token lives in sessionStorage for the tab (not localStorage) and goes only to GitHub's API and the history Worker
why: a token that outlives the tab is a liability for a feature used once per repo
evidence: e2e/history-compute.spec.ts checks Authorization origins and localStorage

decision: the compute offer names the download estimate from the head tree (0.3 MB + 800 B per entry) and warns with download and memory before starting on a big repo (25 MB or more) or a constrained device (deviceMemory 4 GB or less, or a coarse pointer); the button then reads Sign in and compute anyway
why: an 85 MB, 500 MB-of-memory job must not start silently on a phone

decision: history sign-in and compute driven end to end against a fake GitHub and the real Worker in Node (e2e/history-stack.mjs): offer, decline, big-repo warning, popup sign-in, progress, upload, timeline, and a fresh signed-out visitor getting the shared copy
